item.text: {"winner":"A","confidence":"medium","summary":"A is closer to the frozen contract because it preserves Add unchanged and explicitly validates Upload inputs. B has stronger retry coverage, but materially changes Add by eagerly buffering every custom multipart body.","reasons":["A reuses internal/multipartbody.NewFile, produces a replayable body, preserves FilesOption handling, and leaves the lower-level Add API’s behavior intact.","B’s io.ReadAll in Add changes consumption timing, error wrapping, and memory use for all existing Add callers, directly conflicting with the requirement to preserve Add behavior.","B’s changelog and Add retry test confirm that the out-of-scope Add behavior change is intentional rather than incidental.","B tests multipart field, filename, content, and an actual 429 retry much better than A, but neither patch tests validation or source-reader errors as required."],"risks_a":["Upload duplicates Add’s request construction, decoding, and missing-data handling instead of routing through Add, creating divergence risk.","Its Upload test never reads and verifies the uploaded content and does not exercise Upload through a 429 retry.","The added transport test verifies a generic bytes.Reader rather than proving the multipart helper’s Upload body is replayed."],"risks_b":["Add now buffers every caller-provided multipart body in memory and changes reader-error semantics.","Upload calls a new private add helper rather than the existing FilesService.Add method required by the contract.","Upload does not visibly perform filename or nil-content validation itself and has no validation or failing-reader tests."]}
